prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HERMOSILLO, Mexico (CNN)  -- President Felipe Calderon traveled to Hermosillo on Saturday to meet with health officials as the death toll of a day care center fire there grew to 38 children. A crib and baby seats lie outside a day care center Friday in Hermosillo, Mexico, as police cordon off the area. The cause of Friday's blaze remained unknown, but investigators concluded that the fire did not start inside the ABC Day Care, Eduardo Bours, the governor of Sonora state said. As of Saturday night, 23 children remained hospitalized, 15 of them in critical condition, Sonora spokesman Daniel Duran told CNN. Another 10 children had been transported to other hospitals: eight to Guadalajara, one to Ciudad Obregon, and one to Sacramento, California. A team of 29 medical experts in Hermosillo were deciding if any more victims would be moved to the Shriners Hospital in Sacramento, or elsewhere. In addition, six adults were injured, Duran said. "Without a doubt this is the worst disaster we've had," Bours told CNN. The president arrived with Interior Secretary Fernando Gomez Mont and Health Secretary Jose Angel Cordova to get firsthand updates from doctors and investigators, the state news agency Notimex reported. Calderon ordered the nation's attorney general to investigate the blaze. Most of the victims died from smoke inhalation and not burns, Bours said. But the fire was enough for the roof to collapse, he added. At the time of the blaze, 142 children were inside the ABC Day Care. The day care is for children ages 2 to 4, but Bours confirmed that children even younger were among the victims. All the children at the day care had been accounted for by Saturday evening, Bours said. A severely burned 3-year-old girl arrived Saturday at the Sacramento hospital -- where pediatric burn treatment is a specialty -- and was in critical condition, according to Dr. Tina Palmieri, assistant chief of the burn unit. The child was burned over 80 percent of her body, the doctor told reporters. She said the hospital normally can save just over half of the children with burns that severe. In Hermosillo, a large crowd gathered outside of the emergency entrance of the city's general hospital and many people consoled each other, video from the scene showed. "They told me that this happened in a matter of five minutes," Hermosillo Mayor Ernesto Gandara told reporters after surveying the scene.

On Friday, a crib and infant seats could be seen outside the Hermosillo day care facility while police kept the area sealed off. The origin of the fire that broke out Friday was still not known, but investigators determined it had not begun inside ABC Day Care, according to Sonora Gov. Eduardo Bours.

By Saturday night, 23 children were still being treated in hospitals, including 15 who were listed in critical condition, Sonora spokesman Daniel Duran told CNN. Ten other children had been transferred to hospitals elsewhere: eight to Guadalajara, one to Ciudad Obregon and one to Sacramento, California. In Hermosillo, a group of 29 medical specialists was assessing whether additional victims should be sent to Shriners Hospital in Sacramento or to other facilities. Duran also said six adults were hurt.

“This is without question the worst tragedy we have experienced,” Bours told CNN.

According to the state news agency Notimex, Calderon arrived with Interior Secretary Fernando Gomez Mont and Health Secretary Jose Angel Cordova so they could receive direct briefings from physicians and investigators. Calderon also instructed Mexico’s attorney general to look into the fire.

There were 142 children inside ABC Day Care when the fire started. The facility serves children between the ages of 2 and 4, but Bours confirmed that some victims were even younger. By Saturday evening, all children who had been at the center had been located, he said.

A 3-year-old girl with severe burns was flown Saturday to the Sacramento hospital, which specializes in pediatric burn care. Dr. Tina Palmieri, assistant chief of the burn unit, said the girl was in critical condition. In Hermosillo, video showed a large gathering outside the emergency entrance of the city’s general hospital, where many people comforted one another.

“They told me this all happened in about five minutes,” Hermosillo Mayor Ernesto Gandara said to reporters after visiting the site.

The blaze broke out on **June 5, 2009**, at a facility that cared for young children under a contract with Mexico’s Social Security Institute, known as the **IMSS**. Most of the victims were toddlers and preschool-age children. Authorities said **more than 70 children were injured**, many suffering severe burns and smoke inhalation.

Witnesses and parents described scenes of chaos as firefighters, neighbors and rescuers tried to break through walls and windows to reach trapped children. The fire was believed to have started in or near an adjoining government-leased warehouse before spreading rapidly into the day care center.

Sonora state officials also pledged a full inquiry, while IMSS officials said they would review safety conditions at contracted child-care centers nationwide.

Children were moved to medical centers in cities including **Guadalajara** and **Mexico City**, and several were flown to the **United States** for advanced burn treatment, including care at specialized pediatric hospitals.

The disaster prompted national outrage over safety inspections, emergency exits and the outsourcing of public child-care services. Families of the victims demanded accountability, saying the children were left in a building that lacked adequate protections against fire.

The ABC Day Care fire remains a defining tragedy in Mexico, remembered not only for its devastating death toll but also for the questions it raised about government oversight and the safety of children in public-supported facilities.

**Calderón Visits Hermosillo After Deadly Day Care Fire That Killed Dozens of Children**

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico —** President Felipe Calderón traveled to the northern city of Hermosillo, Sonora, in the aftermath of one of Mexico’s deadliest child-care tragedies, as grieving families demanded answers over a fire at the Guardería ABC day care center that killed dozens of young children and injured many more.

The blaze, which broke out on June 5, 2009, tore through the privately operated day care facility while children were inside for the day. The center provided services under contract with Mexico’s Social Security Institute, known as the IMSS. Most of the victims were toddlers and preschool-age children, and many of those who survived suffered severe burns and smoke inhalation.

Calderón’s visit came amid mounting public outrage over the conditions at the facility, questions about emergency preparedness, and accusations that government oversight had failed to protect the children.

During his visit, Calderón met with families of victims and injured children, as well as state and local officials. He promised a thorough investigation and said those responsible would be held accountable. The president also pledged federal support for medical care, including specialized treatment for burn victims, some of whom were transferred to hospitals in other parts of Mexico and the United States.

“This is a tragedy that has wounded all of Mexico,” Calderón said in remarks at the time, expressing condolences to the families. He said federal authorities would assist in determining how the fire spread so quickly and why the children could not be evacuated in time.

According to early reports, the fire may have started in an adjacent warehouse or storage area and spread into the day care center. Witnesses described desperate scenes as parents, neighbors, firefighters and emergency workers tried to break through walls and pull children from the smoke-filled building. Some rescuers used vehicles to ram openings into the structure in an effort to reach those trapped inside.

The tragedy quickly raised serious concerns about building safety. Reports indicated that the day care center lacked adequate emergency exits and that flammable materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of smoke and flames. Families questioned how the facility had been allowed to operate despite apparent safety risks.

The fire became a national scandal not only because of the number of children killed, but also because of the day care center’s ties to the government-run social security system. Guardería ABC was part of a network of privately managed child-care centers contracted by the IMSS to serve working parents. After the fire, critics argued that outsourcing child care had created gaps in accountability and inspections.

Parents of the victims demanded justice, calling for criminal charges against owners, officials and inspectors who may have ignored safety violations. Demonstrations were held in Hermosillo and other cities, with mourners carrying photographs of the children and banners demanding punishment for negligence.

Calderón ordered federal agencies to review safety standards at day care centers across the country. The IMSS also came under intense scrutiny, and officials promised to cooperate with investigators. Sonora state authorities opened their own inquiries, while federal prosecutors examined whether negligence or corruption had played a role.

The disaster remains one of the most painful episodes in modern Mexican history. In total, 49 children died from the fire and its aftermath, and more than 100 were injured. Many survivors and families continued for years to seek medical support, compensation and legal accountability.

For the families in Hermosillo, Calderón’s visit was only the beginning of a long struggle. While federal officials promised justice, parents insisted that condolences and investigations were not enough.

“They were children,” one grieving parent said in the days after the fire. “They were left in a place that should have been safe.”
